subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]
passage: Okay, so in Class Ten I was sure everyone hated me. It started in the canteen queue: three girls from my section looked at me, looked at each other, then looked away. I went home certain they were laughing at my haircut. For two days I sat at the back and wouldn't lift my eyes. Then you, Wasim, cornered me at the water cooler and said, "Suraj, why are you avoiding everybody?" I told you. You said, "Just ask them, yaar." So I did, red in the face. One of them said, "We wanted you on our quiz team but we were too shy to ask." 😅 I've never felt so silly. Now I check before I decide.

qa.q: Where did the three girls look at Suraj and then away?
qa.a: They looked at Suraj in the canteen queue.

qa.q: Why did Suraj sit at the back and not lift Suraj's eyes for two days?
qa.a: Suraj was certain the girls were laughing at the haircut, and felt embarrassed and wanted to avoid being looked at. The glances could have meant many things, but the worst was all that got imagined.

qa.q: What could Suraj do the next time someone glances at Suraj and looks away?
qa.a: Suraj could check the facts first, by asking a friend or the person kindly, before deciding it means gossip. Asking took Suraj two days to try but cleared it up in a minute.

qa.q: How might the girls have felt while they were looking and looking away?
qa.a: They were shy about inviting Suraj to the quiz team, so looking away was nervousness, not judgement. They may not have known Suraj was watching them.

grounding: A teenager reads sideways glances as gossip, then checks the facts and finds shyness.

subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]
passage: I sit behind Abhinav in maths, so I saw the whole thing. Some girls by the window kept glancing over during the test review, and he noticed. His shoulders went up and his pen stopped moving. At lunch he muttered, "They're talking about my marks." I said, "Or your shirt, or nothing." He nearly walked off. Then he went straight over and asked, "Were you looking at me?" One girl said, "Your pencil box has the same sticker as mine, I wanted to ask where you got it." He laughed and his shoulders dropped. I'm Yusuf, and I can't say what was going on inside him, but I think he'd been scared for two periods.

qa.q: Where do Yusuf and Abhinav sit in relation to each other in maths?
qa.a: Yusuf sits behind Abhinav in maths.

qa.q: What was Abhinav probably worried about when he saw the glances?
qa.a: He probably worried the girls were talking about his marks. His raised shoulders and stopped pen fit that, though Yusuf admits he cannot know for sure.

qa.q: What could Abhinav try if he notices glances again?
qa.a: He can do what he did at lunch: ask calmly whether they were looking at him, and hear the reason before assuming. A friend nearby can also offer other possible reasons.

qa.q: How does the girl by the window see the situation?
qa.a: She was only curious about the sticker and wanted to ask about it. She may have been surprised that a glance caused worry.

grounding: A teenager reads sideways glances as gossip, and asking directly shows a harmless reason, as seen by an observer.

subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]
passage:
Monday: In the corridor, Francis caught Akash and two other boys glancing sideways at him, then leaning in to whisper. Francis touched his new, too-short haircut. Great. They were laughing at it.
Wednesday: Francis avoided Akash all day. When Akash asked to borrow a protractor, Francis snapped, "Ask your gossip club." Akash looked stunned and walked off.
Friday: Francis was still stewing when Akash came up to him at the bus stop, rubbing the back of his neck. "Okay, I'll just say it. We need a fourth person for the inter-school quiz. We kept looking at you all week because nobody had the guts to ask."
Francis stared at him. All that, for a quiz?
"I thought you were laughing at my hair," he admitted.
Akash snorted. "Your hair is terrible. But you know all the capitals."

qa.q: What did Akash's group need a fourth person for?
qa.a: The inter-school quiz.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he snapped at Akash on Wednesday?
qa.a: Francis felt hurt and self-conscious, sure that the sideways glances meant the group was mocking his haircut.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could have fixed it sooner?
qa.a: Francis assumed the worst from glances and turned cold; asking Akash directly on Monday would have cleared it up before the snapping.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when Francis snapped at him?
qa.a: Akash probably felt confused and stung, since the glances were shy attempts to ask Francis to join, not gossip.

grounding: Across a week, a teenager reads peers' sideways glances as gossip, causes needless conflict, then learns they came from shyness.

subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]
passage:
"Ayesha, you think everyone in your class is whispering about you? Let your Lokesh Chacha tell you something.
When I was fifteen, my shoes had a big split at the toe. Every time I walked into class, I saw Prakash and his friends glance sideways and mutter. I was sure it was about my shoes. For a whole month I sat with my feet tucked under the bench.
One day I lost my temper. I marched up and said, 'Say it to my face.' Prakash looked terrified. 'Say what? We were looking at the clock above your seat. We were counting down to the bell.'
The clock. For a month I had been fighting a clock.
So before you decide what a glance means, check."

qa.q: Where was the clock that Prakash's group kept looking at?
qa.a: Above Lokesh's seat.

qa.q: What was young Lokesh feeling during that month?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and self-conscious about his split shoes, sure the glances were mocking him, which built up into anger.

qa.q: What choice inside the story led to needless conflict?
qa.a: Lokesh chose to assume the worst for a month and then confront Prakash angrily instead of calmly checking what the glances meant.

qa.q: How might Prakash have felt when Lokesh marched up to him?
qa.a: Prakash was probably frightened and confused, since he had only been watching the clock.

grounding: An uncle recalls reading sideways glances as judgement about his shoes and learning to check the facts before assuming.

subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]
passage:
The final exam hall was dead silent, with an invigilator pacing between rows. Hemant was halfway through the physics paper when he noticed Zubin, two seats to his left, glancing sideways at him. Once. Twice. Five times.
Was Zubin trying to copy? Was he judging how slowly Hemant was writing? Hemant hunched over his paper and covered it with his arm, his neck prickling.
He couldn't whisper or ask. He just had to keep writing.
Outside, after the bell, Hemant said stiffly, "Why were you staring at me?"
Zubin looked blank. Then he laughed. "Not at you. At the wall clock behind you. My watch died this morning, and I was panicking about time."
Hemant turned around. There was the clock, right above where he had been sitting.

qa.q: Why was Zubin glancing in Hemant's direction?
qa.a: He was looking at the wall clock behind Hemant because his watch had died.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling as he covered his paper?
qa.a: Hemant felt uneasy and suspicious, reading the glances as copying or judgement, which made his neck prickle.

qa.q: What did Hemant do after the exam that helped?
qa.a: He asked Zubin directly instead of carrying the suspicion, which showed the glances were about the clock.

qa.q: What would change if Hemant had reported Zubin for copying?
qa.a: Zubin could have been wrongly accused and hurt, all because of a glance that meant something else.

grounding: In a silent exam hall, a teenager reads a peer's sideways glances as copying, then checks and learns they were about time.

subtype: Sideways glance and shifting gaze in peer groups [Interpreting]
passage: On Monday morning in the corridor of her Bengaluru school, Vidya caught Irawati glancing at her sideways and then quickly looking at the floor. Irawati leaned towards Shreya and whispered. Vidya's face went hot. It had to be the fringe; she had cut it herself on Sunday. All through maths she drafted a sharp message in her head. At lunch she nearly walked past their table without a word. Instead she stopped. "Irawati, were you two talking about me this morning?" Irawati turned red. "Sort of. We wanted to ask if you'd sing in our band for the fest. I didn't know how to ask, so I kept looking and then lost my nerve." Shreya laughed. "She practised the question three times." Vidya sat down slowly, the sharp message gone.

qa.q: When had Vidya cut her fringe?
qa.a: On Sunday.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling when her face went hot?
qa.a: Vidya felt embarrassed and angry, sure that Irawati was whispering about the home-cut fringe.

qa.q: What stopped this from turning into a needless fight?
qa.a: Vidya asked Irawati directly instead of sending the sharp message or walking past, and the real reason came out 🙂

qa.q: How did Irawati experience that morning?
qa.a: Irawati was shy and nervous about asking Vidya to sing, so she kept glancing over and then lost her nerve.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager reading sideways glances as gossip when they came from shyness, and checking the facts instead of assuming the worst.
